guides.name: Italian Game
guides.mainline: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Bc5 4. c3 Nf6 5. d3 d6 6. O-O
guides.idea: White develop the bishop to c4, targeting f7, and prepare a pawn center with c3 and d4. Black respond symmetrically and try to keep White's queen and knight away from the kingside.
white: Develop before launching an attack: Nf3, Bc4, c3 and d4.
Watch f7, a frequent target for tactical strikes.
Do not rush d4 before castling.
black: Place the bishop on c5 and knight on f6 to put pressure on e4.
Play ...d6 and ...O-O, then prepare ...a6 and ...b5.
Watch for Nxe5 and a fork on f7.
mistakes: Calculate early attacks on f7: one bishop usually does not create a decisive threat.
Before d4, check ...exd4 and the pressure on e4.

guides.idea: White put pressure on the c6-knight, which defends e5. This indirectly challenges the center: Black must consider Bxc6 followed by Nxe5. A long positional struggle often follows.
white: Retreat the bishop to b3 and prepare c3 and d4.
Use Re1 to contest the e-file.
Prepare Nbd2–f1–g3 for a kingside attack.
black: Use ...a6 and ...b5 to drive the bishop back.

mistakes: In the Exchange Variation, Bxc6 does not always win e5: ...Qd4 may answer Nxe5.

black: After ...dxc4, develop and challenge the center with ...c5 or ...e5.

mistakes: After 1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4 3.e3 b5?! 4.a4, Black's pawn chain needs concrete defensive moves.
Do not leave the king in the center while trying to recover every pawn immediately.

guides.name: Basic checkmates
guides.mainline: 1. e4 e5 2. Bc4 Nc6 3. Qh5 Nf6 4. Qxf7#
notes: White moves the pawn from e2 to e4. The move occupies the central square e4. From e4, it controls d5. It opens a diagonal for the bishop on f1.
Black moves the pawn from e7 to e5. The move occupies the central square e5. From e5, it controls d4. It opens a diagonal for the bishop on f8.

White moves the bishop from f1 to c4. This develops a piece from its starting rank. From c4, it controls d5. It attacks enemy pieces or pawns on f7; whether a capture is possible depends on the reply and any pins.
Black moves the knight from b8 to c6. This develops a piece from its starting rank. From c6, it controls d4, e5.
White moves the queen from d1 to h5. From h5, it controls e5. It attacks enemy pieces or pawns on e5, f7, h7; whether a capture is possible depends on the reply and any pins.

Black moves the knight from g8 to f6. This develops a piece from its starting rank. From f6, it controls e4, d5. It attacks enemy pieces or pawns on e4, h5; whether a capture is possible depends on the reply and any pins.

White moves the queen from h5 to f7 and captures the pawn. From f7, it controls d5. It attacks enemy pieces or pawns on f6, d7, g7, f8; whether a capture is possible depends on the reply and any pins. Checkmate: the king has no legal way to escape check. The queen captures f7 with support from the bishop on c4. The king cannot capture the protected queen or block an adjacent check. Defend f7 while developing; after Qh5, ...g6 is one possible defense.
guides.idea: Learn eleven named mating patterns: three opening traps from the starting position and eight simplified setup positions. Each line ends in checkmate. The traps illustrate defensive mistakes, not forced wins against correct play.
white: Before checking, count every escape square and possible capture.
Coordinate the attacking pieces: a protected checking piece is often essential.
black: Watch the weak f7 square and avoid exposing the e8–h5 diagonal.
Give the king an escape square when the back rank becomes vulnerable.
mistakes: A threat is not mate: check captures, blocks and king moves.
Setup positions teach a pattern; they are not continuations of the opening traps.

variations.name: Fool's mate
notes: White moves the pawn from f2 to f3. From f3, it controls e4.
Black moves the pawn from e7 to e5. The move occupies the central square e5. From e5, it controls d4. It opens a diagonal for the bishop on f8.
White moves the pawn from g2 to g4. From its new square, it controls f5, h5.

Black moves the queen from d8 to h4. From its new square, it controls e1, f2, h2, g3 and other squares. It attacks enemy pieces or pawns on h2, g4; whether a capture is possible depends on the reply and any pins. Checkmate: the king has no legal way to escape check. The moves f3 and g4 expose the h4–e1 diagonal. The queen mates while White's own pieces block the king's escape squares. Avoid weakening this diagonal without calculating the consequences.

The knight on d5 gives mate: Ne5 covers d7, Bf7 covers e8 and e6, and Black's own pieces block the remaining escapes. Taking the queen on d1 loses; Black should instead consider ...dxe5.

variations.name: Back-rank mate (setup position)
notes: White moves the rook from a1 to a8. From its new square, it controls a1, a2, a3, a4 and other squares. Checkmate: the king has no legal way to escape check. The rook invades the eighth rank. Pawns on f7, g7 and h7 prevent the king from moving down, while the rook controls the entire rank. Check whether your king has a safe escape square before leaving the back rank undefended.

variations.name: Smothered mate (setup position)
notes: White moves the knight from h6 to f7. From f7, it controls e5. Checkmate: the king has no legal way to escape check. The knight on f7 attacks h8. Black's rook on g8 and pawns on g7 and h7 trap their own king; a knight check cannot be blocked. An escape square had to be created before this move.

variations.name: Arabian mate (setup position)
notes: White moves the rook from a7 to h7. From its new square, it controls h1, h2, h3, h4 and other squares. Checkmate: the king has no legal way to escape check. The rook on h7 checks along the h-file, while the knight on f6 protects the rook and controls g8. The rook covers g7, so the rook and knight together trap the king in the corner.

variations.name: Anastasia's mate (setup position)
notes: White moves the rook from a5 to h5. From h5, it controls d5, e5. Checkmate: the king has no legal way to escape check. The rook on h5 controls the h-file. The knight on e7 covers g8 and g6, and Black's own pawn on g7 blocks the last escape. In this pattern, the knight keeps the king on the edge of the board.

variations.name: Boden's mate (setup position)
notes: White moves the bishop from c4 to a6. From its new square, it controls f1, e2, d3, c4 and other squares. Checkmate: the king has no legal way to escape check. The bishop on a6 checks along a6–c8, while the bishop on f4 covers b8 and c7. The rook on d8 and pawn on d7 obstruct their own king: the two bishops seal the escapes on crossing diagonals.

variations.name: Epaulette mate (setup position)
notes: White moves the queen from b3 to e6. From e6, it controls e4, d5, e5. Checkmate: the king has no legal way to escape check. The queen on e6 controls e8 and the nearby squares on the seventh rank. Black's own rooks on d8 and f8 act like epaulettes, blocking sideways escapes. The king has no safe square.

variations.name: Dovetail mate (setup position)
notes: White moves the queen from h4 to e7. From its new square, it controls b4, h4, c5, g5 and other squares. Checkmate: the king has no legal way to escape check. The queen on e7 gives an adjacent check and is protected by the bishop on b4. Black's own rooks on d5 and f5 occupy the two diagonal escape squares behind the king that the queen does not control. These two obstructions form the dovetail pattern.

variations.name: Ladder mate (setup position)
notes: White moves the rook from b1 to b8. From its new square, it controls b1, b2, b3, b4 and other squares. Checkmate: the king has no legal way to escape check. The rook on b8 checks along the eighth rank, while the rook on a7 cuts off the seventh. Rooks take away successive ranks like steps of a ladder; keep each rook out of the enemy king's reach.

guides.idea: Nxf7 sacrifices a knight on a fork square: after ...Kxf7 and Qf3+, Black's king must help defend the d5-knight.
white: White should develop Nc3 against d5 while Black's king remains in the center.
black: Black must calculate checks and attacks on d5 before trying to keep the extra material.
mistakes: Black can choose 5...Na5 instead of 5...Nxd5; Nxf7 is not forced in the Two Knights Defense.

guides.name: Halloween Gambit
guides.mainline: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. Nxe5 Nxe5 5. d4 Ng6 6. e5 Ng8 7. Bc4 Bb4 8. Qf3 f5
guides.idea: Nxe5 gives a knight for a pawn so that ...Nxe5 and d4 allow White to chase Black's knights with pawns.
white: White should use the tempi from d4 and e5 to develop rather than only push pawns.
black: Black should find safe knight squares and a timely ...d5 break.
mistakes: Gaining tempi does not replace the sacrificed piece; the gambit needs concrete calculation.

guides.name: Two Knights Defense, Traxler
match: Italian Game: Two Knights Defense, Traxler
guides.mainline: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Nf6 4. Ng5 Bc5
guides.idea: Instead of defending f7, Black play ...Bc5 and prepare a bishop sacrifice on f2 with check.
white: White should compare Bxf7+ and Nxf7, taking ...Bxf2+ into account.
black: Black need forcing play: losing a queen or rook without checks is dangerous.
mistakes: Capturing the bishop with Kxf2 allows further checks; declining the sacrifice must also be calculated.

guides.mainline: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 Nc6 4. Nxc6 dxc6
guides.idea: With ...Nc6 Black offer the e5-pawn for development; ...dxc6 opens bishop diagonals.

black: Black need active bishop development before White finish castling.

guides.name: Evans Gambit
guides.mainline: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Bc5 4. b4 Bxb4
guides.idea: The move b4 deflects the c5-bishop: after ...Bxb4, c3 gains a tempo to prepare d4.
white: White should castle quickly and open the center while Black's bishop spends tempi moving.
black: Black should finish development, returning the pawn if necessary.
mistakes: The b4-pawn does not force ...Bxb4; ...Bb6 changes the structure and plans.

guides.mainline: 1. e4 c5 2. d4 cxd4 3. c3 dxc3 4. Nxc3 Nc6 5. Bc4 e6 6. Nf3 d6 7. O-O a6 8. Qe2 b5 9. Bb3 Ra7
guides.idea: The move c3 offers another central pawn: after ...dxc3 and Nxc3, White develop with open c- and d-files.
white: White can use Bc4, Nf3 and castling, followed by pressure against d6.
black: Black should choose an ...e6/...d6 setup or a fianchetto without leaving the king in the center.
mistakes: If Black decline ...dxc3, the plans of the accepted gambit do not automatically apply.

guides.name: Wing Gambit
guides.mainline: 1. e4 c5 2. b4 cxb4 3. a3 d5 4. exd5 Qxd5 5. Bb2
guides.idea: The move b4 draws the c5-pawn away from the center, offering material for d4 and open lines.
white: White should compare immediate d4 with a3, attacking the b4-pawn again.
black: Black should examine the central ...d5 break before trying to keep every pawn.
mistakes: After a3, ...bxa3 is optional; central action may matter more than collecting pawns.

guides.name: Albin Countergambit
guides.mainline: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e5 3. dxe5 d4 4. Nf3 Nc6 5. Nbd2 Qe7
guides.idea: After ...e5 and dxe5, ...d4 establishes an advanced pawn that disrupts White's usual development.
white: White should develop Nf3 and choose when to attack the d4-pawn.
black: Black can support d4 with ...Nc6 and active piece play.
mistakes: An early e3 requires checking ...Bb4+ and ...dxe3, the basis of the Lasker Trap.

guides.mainline: 1. d4 d5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. e3 g6 4. Bd3 Bg7
guides.idea: White build a d4-e3 center and prepare e4 with Bd3, Nf3 and Nbd2.

black: Black can play a timely ...c5 or develop the c8-bishop before ...e6.
mistakes: An attack on h7 needs calculation; a bishop on d3 alone does not justify Bxh7+.

guides.name: Englund Gambit
guides.mainline: 1. d4 e5 2. dxe5 Nc6 3. Nf3 Qe7
guides.idea: The move ...e5 offers a pawn against d4; after dxe5, Black seek tempi with ...Nc6 and queen moves.
white: White should develop while watching checks along the a5-e1 diagonal.
black: Black must calculate queen threats without neglecting kingside development.
mistakes: An early queen attack may gain a tempo but also lets White develop while attacking the queen.

guides.idea: The move ...d5 challenges the center immediately after Nf3, allowing captures on d5 or e5.
white: White should compare exd5 and Nxe5, checking ...e4 attacks against the knight.
black: Black should turn central tempi into development rather than only push pawns.
mistakes: After central pawn exchanges, the open e-file can endanger either king.

guides.name: St. George Defense
guides.mainline: 1. e4 a6 2. d4 b5 3. Nf3 Bb7 4. Bd3 e6
guides.idea: The move ...a6 prepares ...b5 and ...Bb7, but gives White time to occupy the center.
white: White can occupy d4 and e4, then finish development before opening the position.
black: Black should combine ...Bb7 with a ...c5 or ...d5 break.
mistakes: Flank pawn moves without central action let White gain space.

guides.name: Vienna Gambit
guides.mainline: 1. e4 e5 2. Nc3 Nf6 3. f4 d5 4. fxe5 Nxe4 5. Qf3 f5
guides.idea: The move f4 after Nc3 challenges e5 and opens the f-file at the cost of king safety.
white: White should check the central ...d5 reply and develop the g1-knight in time.
black: Black should compare capturing on f4 with the ...d5 counterstrike.
mistakes: After f4, checks along h4-e1 need attention even with a knight on c3.

Black moves the knight from f6 to e4 and captures the pawn. The move occupies the central square e4. From its new square, it controls d2, f2, c3, g3 and other squares. It attacks enemy pieces or pawns on d2, c3; whether a capture is possible depends on the reply and any pins.
